summary: Describes an authentication option for the Telnet protocol: a generic method to negotiate an authentication type and mode, including whether to encrypt and whether to forward credentials.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet sends your password across the network in readable form. This document defines a Telnet option that fixes that: the client and server first agree on how to prove who they are, and can then encrypt the rest of the session.

questions: how do you encrypt a telnet session
what is the telnet auth modifier
subtitle: How a Telnet client and server agree on a way to prove identity, switch on encryption and pass credentials along.

tldr.problem: Telnet sends passwords in clear text across the network, so anyone watching the packets can read them.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a Telnet option, number 37, that negotiates an authentication method before any data is sent. The option carries a type pair that says who authenticates whom, whether the exchange is one-way or mutual, whether encryption is wanted, and whether the client will forward credentials.
tldr.outcome: A client can prove its identity without typing a password, and the session can be encrypted once authentication succeeds. The document updated the earlier version, RFC 1416, so that it can drive the Telnet encryption option.

today: RFC 2941 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It updated RFC 1416 in 2000 so that the option could drive the Telnet encryption option, defined in RFC 2946, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: The Option, Its Commands and Its Types
sections.content:
The AUTHENTICATION option is Telnet option number 37. It defines four subcommands: IS, which is 0 and carries authentication information from the client; SEND, which is 1 and is a server's request for that information; REPLY, which is 2 and is the server's answer; and NAME, which is 3 and carries the account name the user wants to use on the remote host.

The document lists the authentication types that have been assigned. NULL is 0, KERBEROS_V4 is 1, KERBEROS_V5 is 2, SPX is 3, MINK is 4, SRP is 5, RSA is 6, SSL is 7, LOKI is 10, SSA is 11, KEA_SJ is 12, KEA_SJ_INTEG is 13, DSS is 14 and NTLM is 15. Numbers 8 and 9 are unassigned. The types marked with an asterisk in the document were never submitted to the IETF for consideration as an Internet standard.

The document defines the framework only. It does not define a specific authentication type; separate documents describe each one. Future type numbers and modifiers are assigned by the IANA under a first-come first-served policy, and IANA is instructed not to issue new suboption values without documentation of their use.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is number 37 in Telnet's list. It has four subcommands: ask for credentials, send them, answer, and name the account. The document lists the authentication methods that have numbers, but does not define any of them.

sections.title: Why Telnet Needed This
sections.content:
One of the deficiencies of the Telnet protocol is that to log into a remote system, users type their passwords, which pass in clear text through the network. If the connection crosses an untrusted network, someone watching the packets can read the passwords.

The purpose of the AUTHENTICATION option is to provide a framework for passing authentication information through the Telnet session, and a mechanism to enable encryption of the data stream as a side effect of successful authentication or through the separate Telnet ENCRYPT option. The document sets out three results. The user's password is not sent in clear text across the network. If the front-end Telnet process holds the right authentication information, it can send it automatically and the user types no password at all. And once authentication has succeeded, the data stream can be encrypted, which protects against active attackers.

The intent is that the option be general enough to carry information for any authentication and encryption system.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet has always asked for a password and sent it in the open. This option gives the client a way to prove itself instead, and a way to switch the session to encrypted mode once that proof has been made.

sections.title: The Commands and the Type Pair
sections.content:
The client sends WILL AUTHENTICATION to say it is willing to send and receive authentication information, and the server sends DO AUTHENTICATION to say the same. If the client refuses, it sends WONT and the server must answer with DONT; if the server refuses, it sends DONT and the client must answer with WONT.

The server asks for credentials with IAC SB AUTHENTICATION SEND authentication-type-pair-list IAC SE, where the list is an ordered list of type pairs. Only the server may send it. The client answers with IAC SB AUTHENTICATION IS authentication-type-pair auth-data IAC SE, and the server replies with IAC SB AUTHENTICATION REPLY authentication-type-pair auth-data IAC SE. The optional IAC SB AUTHENTICATION NAME remote-user IAC SE names the account the user wants to be authorised to use; authentication may still succeed while that authorisation fails.

The type pair is two octets: the first is the authentication type and the second is a modifier. A type may or may not include encryption of its own. Kerberos 4, for example, needs the separate Telnet ENCRYPT option, while SSL and KEA_SJ provide an encrypted channel as part of a successful negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: The server asks, the client answers, and the server replies. Each of those messages carries a two-octet pair: which method, and a modifier that says how it should be used.

sections.title: The Modifier Bits
sections.content:
There are five one-bit fields in the modifier. The first two, the AUTH_WHO_MASK bit and the AUTH_HOW_MASK bit, are processed as a pair and give four combinations. AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER with AUTH_HOW_ONE_WAY means the client sends information about the local user and the server authenticates that user. AUTH_SERVER_TO_CLIENT with AUTH_HOW_ONE_WAY means the server authenticates itself to the client, so the client knows it is talking to the right server. With AUTH_HOW_MUTUAL, both sides take part, in whichever order the AUTH_WHO bit implies.

The third and fifth bits are the ENCRYPT_MASK bits, which say whether and how encryption is enabled. ENCRYPT_OFF means no encryption, and the Telnet ENCRYPT option should not be negotiated; this mode must be used with all authentication types that do not provide a shared secret to use as a session key. ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT means encryption is negotiated through the Telnet ENCRYPT option, which must be negotiated in both directions immediately after authentication completes, before credentials are forwarded, before other options are negotiated and before any user data is sent; a failure in either direction must terminate the session at once. ENCRYPT_AFTER_EXCHANGE means encryption starts in both directions right after the shared session key has been exchanged, with the algorithm implied by the authentication type.

The fourth bit is the INI_CRED_FWD_MASK bit, which is set by the client to advise the server to expect forwarded credentials. Credentials must not be forwarded if AUTH_CLIENT_TO_SERVER with AUTH_HOW_ONE_WAY was used, because the identity of the server cannot be assured, and should not be forwarded if the connection is not protected by encryption or integrity protection. It is a protocol error to set this bit when the authentication mechanism cannot forward credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: The modifier says four things: who proves their identity, whether both sides do, whether the session gets encrypted, and whether the client will send the credentials on. Those choices decide how much protection the session ends up with.

sections.title: Rules for the Negotiation
sections.content:
WILL and DO are used only at the beginning of the connection, to obtain and grant permission for later negotiation. The option is negotiated in one direction only: the server must send the DO and the client must send the WILL. The reason is that there are three cases, server authenticates client, client authenticates server, and both authenticate each other, and the suboption says which one applies. If the server receives a DO it must respond with WONT, and if the client receives a WILL it must respond with DONT.

Once the two hosts have exchanged a DO and a WILL, the server may request authentication information at any time, sending a list of supported types. Only the server may send requests, only the client may send authentication information, and only the server may send replies. As many exchanges as the chosen scheme needs are allowed. If the client supports none of the listed types, it answers with a type of NULL, and the server may then close the connection. When the server concludes that authentication cannot be negotiated, it sends IAC DONT AUTH to the client.

The list of authentication types must be ordered by preference, the first being the most preferred. A server that is WILL AUTH may ask again later, either to check that the client's credentials are still valid or to negotiate a new session key for use during encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the server can ask for credentials, and only the client can send them. The list of acceptable methods is ordered by preference, and the client says NULL when it likes none of them.

sections.title: A Worked Exchange
sections.content:
The document's first example runs with Kerberos 4. The server sends DO AUTHENTICATION and the client answers WILL AUTHENTICATION. The server then asks for authentication with a list offering mutual Kerberos first and one-way Kerberos second, using the type pair KERBEROS_V4 CLIENT|MUTUAL and KERBEROS_V4 CLIENT|ONE_WAY. The client sends the account name with the NAME command, then the IS command carrying the Kerberos ticket. The server replies with REPLY, the type pair and ACCEPT, which states that the authentication succeeded. The client then sends a CHALLENGE to check that it is talking to the right server, and the server answers with a RESPONSE that proves the same thing from its side.

The second example negotiates encryption through the Telnet ENCRYPT option by adding ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT to the type pair. After the challenge and response, both sides negotiate the Telnet ENCRYPT option in each direction for a secure channel, and the connection must be terminated at once if that fails in either direction.

The third example uses integrated encryption with KEA_SJ and the ENCRYPT_AFTER_EXCHANGE modifier. The client sends its KEA certificate and a random value, the server replies with its certificate, its random value and an encrypted nonce, and the client answers with the encrypted combination of the nonces. At that point the client starts encrypting what it sends and the server starts decrypting, and the last exchange is the server's encrypted response, after which the server encrypts its outgoing stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The example shows the whole conversation: agree on the method, send the ticket, get an accept, then a challenge and a response to check both ends are genuine. Two variants add encryption, either through the separate Telnet option or as part of the exchange itself.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Being able to negotiate a common authentication mechanism is a feature that should be used with caution. When the negotiation is performed, no authentication has yet occurred, so each system has no way of knowing whether it is talking to the system it intends. An intruder could try to negotiate a system that is weak or already compromised.

If the authentication type needs encryption to be enabled as a separate optional negotiation, there is a window of vulnerability from the moment authentication completes until the encryption option is turned on, and an active attacker can use it. Offering only type pairs that include ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT closes that window, because both parties agree that the Telnet ENCRYPT option must be negotiated immediately after authentication succeeds. Types that link encryption to successful authentication also protect against the active attacker, and the ENCRYPT_AFTER_EXCHANGE bit lets those types make encryption optional.

A further opening appears when encryption can be turned off and on again without re-authenticating, since an attacker may hijack the stream once encryption is disabled. A client should therefore not support turning encryption off, and if an attempt to re-enable it fails after it was disabled, the client must terminate the connection. The authentication type pair must be integrity protected at the end of the exchange so both ends agree on the result, and each side must verify the consistency of the type pairs in every message received, treating any variation as a fatal protocol error.
sections.plainLanguage: The negotiation itself is not protected, so someone in the middle could force a weaker method than both sides wanted. The document's advice is to only offer methods that switch encryption on immediately, and to end the session if anything about the exchange changes unexpectedly.

sections.title: What the User Should See
sections.content: Protocol specifications do not normally address the user interface, but here the user needs to configure authentication and encryption and to know whether the negotiation succeeded. The user must be able to say whether authentication is to be used, and whether encryption is to be used if authentication succeeds. There should be at least four settings: REQUIRE, which displays an error and terminates the connection if authentication fails; PROMPT, which displays an error and asks the user to confirm before continuing; WARN, which displays an error before continuing; and DISABLE, which does not attempt authentication at all. The encryption switch should have the same settings, though they are only used when authentication succeeds. The default for both switches should be WARN, and the two may be implemented as a single switch, though keeping them separate gives more control.
sections.plainLanguage: The user should be able to choose how strict to be: fail the connection, ask before carrying on, warn and carry on, or switch authentication off. The default is to warn.

messages.note: The server is willing to send and receive authentication information.

messages.label: IAC SB AUTHENTICATION SEND
messages.note: A list of acceptable authentication type pairs, most preferred first.

messages.label: IAC SB AUTHENTICATION NAME
messages.note: The account name the user wants to use.

messages.label: IAC SB AUTHENTICATION IS
messages.note: A CHALLENGE to check that the server is genuine.

messages.label: IAC SB AUTHENTICATION REPLY
messages.note: A RESPONSE that proves the server is genuine.

viz.caption: THE FOUR WHO AND HOW COMBINATIONS

cells: The server has authenticated the user on the client side of the connection.
The client knows it is connected to the server it wants.
The server has authenticated the user, and the client knows it is connected to the right server.
The client knows it is connected to the right server, and the server knows the client is who it claims to be.

items.title: ENCRYPT_OFF
items.text: No encryption. Must be used with types that give no shared secret for a session key.

items.title: ENCRYPT_USING_TELOPT
items.text: The Telnet ENCRYPT option is negotiated in both directions right after authentication, and the session ends at once if that fails.

items.title: ENCRYPT_AFTER_EXCHANGE
items.text: Encryption starts in both directions as soon as the shared session key has been exchanged. The algorithm comes from the authentication type.

items.title: REQUIRE
items.text: Show an error and end the connection if authentication fails.

items.title: PROMPT
items.text: Show an error and ask the user to confirm before continuing.

items.title: WARN
items.text: Show an error and continue. This is the default.

items.title: DISABLE
items.text: Do not attempt authentication at all.
